paragraphs: Will Barnet Interview Edited
All right, so you always stand by for speed.
Sorry to hear that. Yeah.
Well, there's a lot that I'm learning.
These are the things I am not familiar with. Perhaps you ought to put it on so we could talk. We ought to do it casually.

We're rolling now. Actually, I had a number of questions that I want to taste, and just very informally we could talk about it. Just tell me about Maurice Sievan. Well, I can tell you about both his work and the man a little bit. As a man, I always found him to be extremely intense about everything. I mean, extraordinarily sensitive to things. And I think the least little things sort of set him off, it seemed to me, in terms of emotional feelings that were sometimes disturbing. I think he's also a man who no-nonsense sort of person. He wanted things if the thing had to be right for him. He had to feel that this thing was something that what you're saying it's true. And so I think Maurice expect a lot from life in that sense. I also felt that he was in a very real way a very introspective man. In other words, he was very deeply self- involved. And you might say, in a sense, almost a picture of what an artist should be, you know, in terms of perhaps 19th century Romanticism.
You said that he was very intense, and that's the feeling that I get also from hearing about him. Can you give me some examples of maybe conversations you had or things that you might remember?

You know, it's a shame. I mean, I wish, I mean, I think I told you that my memory of Maurice is in bits and starts. You know, I'd meet him at a gallery or I'd see him among some friends, you know. But for some reason, I don't have a sustained vision of him. It's more fragmented. I mean, I was very impressed with the changes in his work as he grew older and how he went into these deep, almost very emotional paintings which were, in a sense, almost all masterish in color and in brush strokes. He went from a more genre to a more visionary kind of art, a larger nature. So

these are the things I remember. There are a lot of other things that have to do with the period he lived in. I mean, he didn't have an easy time, but none of us did. You know, it wasn't a period where there was gold on the streets, lined with gold.
Tell me a little bit about that, what it was like to...

Well, there was a long period of depression in the art world, almost similar to what's happening today in the last past year or so, where nothing financially is happening. And all of us, over the long period that we lived in, very few of us could make a living on our paintings. There were no golden auctions and things of that sort. The art world, it was totally involved. You had to be a very serious artist to be an artist. In other words, you had to be devoted to your work because the only compensation you got was doing your work. And you might say the fact that perhaps a painting would come off very well and you could feel that you accomplished something. The accomplishment was in the work more than anything else. And then, of course, you would like to have your fellow artists and the public enjoy it. That was another problem because when Maurice was developing into maturity, he was overwhelmed by other artists and other movements, you know, although in a very strange way, would you say that? How would you place him in relationship to the expressionist movement?

Well, I was going to ask you that. I've asked other people that and I get different responses from different people. Right. I think his... I personally think that he started freeing himself up around the same time that a lot of other people did, and he started panning from his feelings. Yes, right. Than through his eyes. Right, yes.

That was a big change that took place in his work, and the cameras got bigger and bigger. and more in tune with the time he was working in. However, I always felt, in view of his work, that it was so different than other expressionists. If you want to call him sort of an expressionist, he certainly was a different kind of expressionist, one who I think was closer to the European tradition. There was a sense of pathos that you could feel in his work that you don't feel really in most expressionist work. It's sort of non-objective almost, even though it's supposed to be from the guts. But there's something very non-objective about it. And Maurice had that warm quality in his paint, the way he put the color on, you know, which was sort of almost Rembrandt-like. I think he was trying to make a bigger Rembrandt sometimes than anything else. That was my feeling about him. He was trying to get the, you might say, the insight into humanity through his color and in the mood of his painting. And that was what I got out of it, you know. And I do think he really developed to a point where he, in many ways, you know, fulfilled a lot of his vision.
I think he did I think towards the end also I think he was a little bitter that other people didn't recognize that

well that was another problem that was well the thing is that Maurice was might say committed the same error that so many artists commit and that is that they expect the world to recognize him through their work which very often times, most of the time, is not quite true exactly, if you know what I'm trying to say. In other words, his bitterness came from the fact that he wanted to be able to put a show on, and once he put the show on, that people would recognize that here is a man who is expressing something quite wonderful and should have recognition for it. However, the art world was going in another direction. The art world in the past, say, 50 years, maybe 30 years, 35 years, has been built upon other things, such as a tremendous amount of publicity has to be accompanied by show. You have to be recognized by museums at the same time you're showing. You have to have critics on your side. You have to have younger critics on your side, older critics on your side. You have to have dealers interested in you. That is the way it was done and is being done today. It's not based upon staying in your studio and doing some wonderful work and then coming out with it and showing it and all of a sudden you're recognized that way. It doesn't work that way anymore, unfortunately. It should but it doesn't. And I think that's where Maurice was unable to understand what was going on in a real sense of the word. It was a period, particularly in the last 20s. He died when? In 1981. Well, around the 70s. Pop out is a good example of that. That was a period of the 60s. And he was already doing his work, you see. It was going in the opposite direction of what was being looked upon as being interesting. In other words, an American phenomenon of pop art, that sort of thing. Here he was, a lone individual, romantic, deeply involved with the depth of human drama, and the public wasn't prepared for it. It's unfortunate. Maybe, as you say, time will tell. Well, it certainly needs exposure. Right, right.
They can evaluate it more as time goes on. And values do change, you know, and very often times after the artist dies, not always, they begin to recognize what he's done and the value of it.
Yeah. Can you tell me what kind of person was he?
I thought he was, he had, to me, I mean, I can't really say too much about that. I can only say that I often felt that he was very quick-tempered. and the least little thing would set him off.
Do you have any examples?

Well, there are certain things I think once took place in the gallery and some commotion about some statement made that infuriated Maurice. And I remember his... Could you remember more specifically? Because actually that's very interesting to me because it seems that he knew deep down that he didn't want to sell his paintings and I think he always tried to get out of his relationships with galleries by doing negative things. Yeah, and I heard a story I'll share with you later. If you could remember that. I wish I could give you a detail, and I think I told you I don't have details, unfortunately. Not like Stuart Davis. If you're interviewing me about Stuart Davis, I can give you all the details, because I saw more of him, you see, and it was a little closer to, Or like Joe Solmon in some ways, I understood him much more in terms of over the years. But Maurice, I remember him with Sally Avery, with a certain group of people, sort of an older group, a generation, going to shows and meeting each other and that sort of thing. But we never really had, I don't remember, any evenings where we spent some kind of solid talk. Right. We may have very early, but those I can't recollect. They may have way, way back.
Yeah, yeah.
40's. It's possible.
Did you ever, were you ever with Maurice with either Milton Avery or with Mark? Sally.
With Sally.

Sally. Most of it was Sally, yeah. Yeah, later on, yeah. What about Mark Rothko? Well, Mark Rothko I knew and saw quite often, but not exactly with Maurice. Sorry about that. Maurice had actually rented his studio in Provincetown. So I'm trying to find any links I can...
Right, yeah. Well, my son also rented Rothko's studio here in the city. Yeah.
But I can't. Now, Provincetown, when was he in Provincetown? In the 50s.
I think I was there at the same time. Did he?

What gallery did he show? He was with HCE, with Ivan Karp. All right. Right. And then there were the Provincetown Art Association. Right. I can't remember. Well, I was in Provincetown in the 50s, too. we had a gallery called I think it was 256 and people like Manzo in it and others but I don't remember Maurice being part of it he was the cop gallery right
yeah can you give me kind of a flavor of what was happening in Provincetown in the late 50s and on Milton Avery

well again Maurice was up against it the big shot was Hans Hoffman and everything in Provincetown was around Hoffman and then later everything was around Motherwell. So Maurice was just one of the other artists working in Provincetown. Right. But was there any kind of scene out there that you could kind of describe or talk about? Well, there were a lot of incidents there that took place. I mean, Provincetown was pretty lively in the 50s, partly due to Hans Hoffman School, which gave it a very exciting flavor, you know. And I think Provincetown at that time was very lively on many levels. The gallery I was in was very lively, you know, showing all new work and so forth. So it was a very thriving art community, I felt. I don't know specifically what I can say about Maurice's relationship to it because I can't remember those things.
Right. That's okay.
I'm sorry.
I'd like to get a little flavor of it.

I would say it was, I think Provincetown was at its height in the 50s. It had great days when Hawthorne was there, too, but I think in the 50s it was extremely lively. I went there every summer for a couple, two or three summers at a house there, and there was a lot of exchange of ideas. Critics were coming in, and I'm sure that Maurice, as far as I can tell, was very much part of that lively group and was involved, Um, but I think basically, uh, Provincetown was largely, the excitement was largely due to the, uh, um, sort of like a little international feeling of Provincetown with Hoffman there and people coming in to, uh, study with him. Grant, um, can you recall any of Maurice's exhibits at all? Are you in the Federation of Modern Painters and Sculptors?

Well, I showed with them all the time. And so we evidently were in a show together for many years. I was a member of the Federation from way back, one of the early members. And we showed up at Riverside, you know, a museum there. I know we showed at other places. Again, I would have to reconstruct my history, you know, to get a flavor of it, you know. But we did show together. And I remember these canvases. I remember these great big canvases with a lot of beautiful sort of brownish Rembrandt-like washes and swirling blacks and grays. But they were all warm on the warm side. And they were very impressive. and very different. And in a sense, they were sort of almost far out in extending their form, you know. So I think, but I always felt that he was a deeply humanistic man, you know, and that my association with him as a fellow artist in consideration of his work was that he was really more of a Rembrandt type than anything else, and that he wasn't particularly contemporary, more back in the past using a more open, abstract kind of way of dealing with his strokes and his shapes, but that he basically was back in Rembrandt's time.

Yeah, I think he studied with Charles Hawthorne and Leon Kroll, and I think that they had really looked into della Francesco's work and the work of the early masters in his schooling. Yes. That would follow, that he would kind of keep that with his...

Well, he wasn't exactly a Piero della Francesco man because he didn't have that light, airy quality. his work had more of a mood feeling, whereas Piero della Francesca has kind of a, I might say, a more formal feeling. I feel that Maurice was what I call informal painter, if you want
me to give you a word for him, which means it's what oftentimes the Europeans way of judging painting between formal and informal.
Right.
Getting through some of these questions. Yeah, I'm sorry. We were just talking, and that was really good. Yeah. Did you ever paint together?
No, we never did. Never painted together.
Can you recall how you met him?
That, again, is difficult. That sort of...
Or how you might have met him.

I think we just, you might say we just simply met at one point, and from then on we knew each other, you know, we were colleagues. But I don't remember any particular time. I don't even remember what year it might have been, to be honest with you. It was probably the 40s, in the 40s.
Late 40s. Yeah. It would have to be the late 40s. Okay. Or not. What was his attitude about life?

Maurice? Well, since I was never that close to him, you know, I could gather by his work, by the way he lived, and by the way he looked at things, that his view of life was of a nature that his art meant everything to him. And that if you were not able to understand his art or appreciate it, that he was very offended by it. That's how I feel about him. That is, his art was Maurice Sievan, and if you didn't accept his art, you were rejecting Maurice Savan. That was my feeling. I think you hit that right on down. And very strongly so, too.
You might have already answered this, but I haven't read that. What are the qualities in his work Speaker 4
that you like?

Well, first, what I liked about his work was his fact that he had an identity. There's no question that it was Maurice's work. It didn't look like so many people in that period that you could hardly tell the difference between one expressionist and another. They're very similar. They use the same colors, everything that the same. With Maurice, it wasn't that way. With Maurice, it was basically a very strong individual feeling about life, you know, that completely was absorbed into his work. In other words, there was a passion. This noise from the television. Are you picking up?
It's loud. Yeah, I am picking it up.
You're picking it up a little bit. So we go and do what you can. Okay. So let's see. Can you give me a kind of historical overview of the art community in the 1940s and then the 1950s?

Yes, I think I can. I think the 40s was very much influenced by the passage of painters coming from Europe, refugees, painters that were having an influence upon the American scene. It was also paired with a war going on. The art world was sort of like a waiting for something. In other words, things came to a standstill sort of. But things were going on all the time, of course. But the war absorbed the life in New York, all over the country for that matter. Things were, we were being absorbed by the war. And even though we were working at the same time, we were always being affected by it. So that I showed, I remember showing in the 40s at the Gallery Saint-Étienne, I think it was 1943, had a big show there. and I remember that there was a strong social feeling about the atmosphere of New York City. In other words, we all felt that, I remember opening the gallery on a Sunday afternoon, feeling that the working people of New York didn't have a chance to see our work during the weekday so they should come on a Sunday when they have a Sunday off. What I'm trying to say is we would try to reach out to the public at that time, you might say almost to the working people with our art, because it wasn't a question of people with money coming in with great sums and buying work. If we could sell a lithograph at that time for $10, it was a big achievement. So you see the art world was in a very, I might say, modest state of being. But I think the forces were forming at that time. In the 40s, I think there were a lot of revolutions going on in New York City among artists. There was this group that just recently we had a show at the Baruch Gallery called Influenced by the Indian Aboriginal Indian Space. I don't know if you know anything about it. So there are a lot of new things coming up. abstraction was becoming more and more prevalent. And we were moving

away from the social period of interest in political statements. And it becoming more and more absorbed, either in the direction of abstraction or a direction in which the combination of a human idea subjected more to being abstracted rather than being shown as a realistic form. In other words, the whole period was imbued with searching for a new way of looking at painting and looking at space, of thinking of form. So in many ways, the 40s was a very important period, very exciting. Just like the 30s was very exciting, but I feel the 30s was not a period of great aesthetic adventure like the 40s. And of course, into the 50s, it was due largely to the 40s, in which we all developed our ideas. I think there was a great surge of individual and conceptual painting that in many ways was way ahead of the Europeans. And that's why I think New York became the center of the art world, because the work we were doing, I think, had a more original concept. And we went beyond Cubism, and we were going beyond surrealism. And a lot of artists were very influenced by the surrealists that came here. You know, a lot of the members were here. Dali was one of them. Of course, they were also influenced by men like Leger that came here and André Lhote, who influenced a lot of students, you know, in abstraction and so forth. So I think the 40s was a rich period despite the war and everything else.
It's funny that you mention André Lhote. Maurice studied with him in Paris in 1931 and 1932. Is there anything in Maurice's work that you can attribute to what he might have learned with André Lhote?

Maybe his earlier work, but certainly not later on. His early work might have had some of the... Lhote was, of course, more of a cubist, you know, in his viewpoints. and I can't exactly say that Maurice was a cubist, you know. I think Maurice was too much of a free spirit to be that way. And I think actually, if you study his work carefully, I haven't seen a whole big show. I'm just going by what I remember, which I'm not, I hope is true enough, but my feeling is that he was basically the same through lifetime in terms of the way he handled a brush. It was a free spirit, free-flowing line. And it just seemed to develop sometimes from a line into a big mass. I think he was always what I call an individual artist.
Okay, that's great. Let's see, what are these I asked?

Does that answer enough the question of the 40s and 50s? Because I do think that 40s and 50s is one of the most crucial periods in American art. I think we did a lot of original work that is not even recognized yet. You see, the school that was recognized was this expressionist school. But there were so many other things going on which were bypassed. And I feel that in the future, they will be able to even out the situation so that Pollock and all the others were not such great originators. There are plenty of others that were just as original and perhaps even

more in some ways. So I think historically, things are going to be very different in 50 years when you go back. Too bad we can't live that long. It would be nice to come back and see what happened. But I'm sure it's going to be very different. See, right now you've got thousands of books on expressionism, but there were all these other painters, such as Maurice, who were working that were not recognized. They were bypassed. Even Davis, in his own way, felt that a little bit.
Right.
You know?
Yeah. Did Maurice Herber discuss things with you like Kierkegaard or metaphysics or other philosophers or poets?

if he did it was only in bits and stats only pieces actually it was hard to get close to Maurice I could only say that I'm trying to recollect the feeling of some of the meetings we had. I remember his face. I remember his eyes. And I remember the intensity of his expressions. But I can't remember the philosophical or any of these profound... Was he a big Kierkegaard man? Yeah, as a matter of fact, he painted...

But see, that's typical of that period. You've got to realize Kierkegaard was a big god at that time. and Maurice was you might say an exponent of it you know I mean there was a period when Nietzsche was a big god too influenced a lot of artists you see there was a period of I guess 1947 where he did a number of conceptual pieces and then his large canvases in the 60s I think he would say Kierkegaard's philosophy probably inspired him to a lot of those pieces.

I wouldn't doubt it. I wouldn't doubt it. He's the sort of man that would be involved with that sort of thing. I think that also had a lot to do with his deepening through his lifetime of, you might say, driving him towards a more extremity of feelings that were hard to handle. Do you know what I mean? And I think that had a lot to do with sometimes creating a situation which led to some of the things that happened to him later in life.
Right. Why do you think Maurice's work never made an impact in the art world? I think that he didn't... In a very simple way, I don't think, first, the galleries that he was in. Name some of them.
Well, he had contemporary arts for two times. He had Albert Landry. He had Passedoit. He had Harry Saltpeter.

Solt Peter, right. He had all those galleries. Now you have your problem, you see. You have the fact that these galleries were not the kind of galleries that commanded attention. So if you showed in those galleries, your reviews are not going to be that extensive, and you're not going to get the public, you're not going to get the critics, you won't even get the museum people. See that's the problem. I think Maurice's problem was very simple. If he had been in a, if say he had been in the Rosenberg Gallery like Milton Avery was in there, it would have made a big difference in his life. That's the way it is. It's that way today, too. It hasn't changed a bit. You get a gallery dealer that has some kind of clout, it's certainly going to do a lot for the artist. And if you're in a gallery that's of a smaller nature, it'll be of a smaller nature. Your extended appreciation will be smaller. It's the way it works. Sorry about that. Yeah, no, that's life, right?

I can only say there's no justice. If you want my final word on the art world or anything else, there is no justice in the world. It shouldn't even be in a dictionary because there's no justice anywhere. I think Maurice felt that too, but he didn't understand it. Right. So let me ask you, when the New York School of Artists came into prominence, Maurice and Lee went to a lot of the 8th Street gatherings, Did you know about that? Oh, yes, I knew all about that. And, you know, Maurice went to all these things because it was sort of exciting, all these guys gathering on a Friday night, you know, and Cedar Bar and getting drunk and calling each other names and things of that sort. Very exciting. And falling off the chairs and things like that. That was a drinking generation, you know. Maurice wasn't that way. Was he a big drinker?
No, actually, I don't think he went to the Cedar Bar all that much. I don't think he did. I know he went to, there was apparently some gathering on 8th Street where a number of, it was a whole

scene for a while, and that was one of the things that he partook in. I think that basically he stayed to himself at the Marines. But I thought maybe if you were there, if you had known him. I don't think he ever felt that he was part of that group. I think he was an outsider that's my feeling and even though he might have gone for interest reasons I think he was closer to the fellow artists that were in the federation at that time like Harry Botkin and others I think he felt closer to these people than he did to the ones in the A Street group that would be my feeling right okay as an artist I think you already said this, but I'll ask it again anyway. As an artist, can you tell me about Sievan's technical abilities and his personal vision? Well, I think from a technical point of view, he always had a style. And it was, you might say, a style that was very indicative of the 19th century painting. In other words, he had a stroke, and that stroke was very meaningful to him, how he presented it. And that stroke extended itself into his work in bigger, bigger forms. So his style was fluid. There was almost a certain amount of virtuosity in it in a very strange way, the way he handled it. And I always felt there was certain luminosity in the work, which I liked. And I felt that the way he put layer and layer of tones on each other were very luminous and had a certain kind of inner drama to them. So in many ways, he was a very successful technician as well as an artist.
And finally, it's been 10 years since his death. What can you say about Maurice Seaband and his arc that would kind of sum it all up?

I would say that he was one of those very individual artists of the period after the war, you know, that someday will be recognized and be placed in history. but it would take time. That's all I can say. And that is that he deserves to be investigated and to try to really understand him so that he gets his due respect and understanding.
That's great. Is there anything else that I didn't cover?
No, that covers it.
That's great. Okay, let's...
(unintelligible)
No. Thank you.
